attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post. He is not quoting anyone.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the mechanism: lab price changes raise short-term revenue but push startups toward open-source models and failure. It leaves out the framing that the labs depend on startups for revenue, but that does not change the commitment. The language is firm ('invariably'), so causal is the right kind.

contract.note: Reading 'these price changes' as the tolls, raw price rises and token-hungry models he lists just before is fair. Requiring the lab price rise to be named as the cause is the ordinary test of his mechanism. Not failing the claim for lack of mass startup deaths is also fair, since he gave no time frame.

evidence.note: Lindy moved all its traffic from Claude to DeepSeek because of cost. That is the direction he described, but no lab price rise is named as the cause.
Says the labs were slower to cut prices, not that they raised them. This weakens the specific causal link, but it does not show prices were cut or held, so the contradiction condition is not met.
Cursor moved to cheaper models such as Kimi and its own Composer, and its margins improved rather than worsening. The article does not tie the move to lab price rises.

reviews.rationale: Startups did move to cheaper open-weight models for cost reasons (Lindy, Cursor). But no item documents an OpenAI or Anthropic price rise for startups that was then named as the cause of a migration or failure. e2 points to slower price cuts, not rises. Nothing shows the labs generally cut or held prices, or that startups stayed put and did well after price rises. The packet does not settle the causal link.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his post, made in his list of 'pale horses'.

semantics.note: A present-tense factual claim that each named startup burns $4 to $5 per $1 of revenue. The proposition keeps the five companies and the ratio.

contract.note: Reading 'burn $4 or $5 per $1' as total spend of about 4 to 5 times revenue is the ordinary reading. Applying it to each company follows from 'these are all'. The period of 2025 to Q1 2026 is a reasonable choice for a present-tense claim.

evidence.note: Gives gross margin figures: Cursor about -23% (reported secondhand by a rival's CEO) and Replit positive. Gross margin is a different metric from total spend per dollar, and the figures come slightly after the target period, so this is context only.
Replit's CEO says, unaudited, that the company was gross margin positive in October 2025. That is a gross margin figure, not total spend or burn relative to revenue.

reviews.rationale: No item gives total spending or cash burn relative to revenue for any of the five companies. The gross margin figures make 4 to 5x look doubtful for Replit and Cursor, but they cannot rule it out, because operating costs are unknown. There are no figures at all for Perplexity, Harvey or Lovable. The packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'It only takes one' is firm language: a single failed exit or firesale is enough to break the illusion. Treating this as a conditional forecast with that event as the antecedent is reasonable. The claim is partly metaphorical, but it is not hedged.

contract.note: Reading 'break the illusion' as broad AI-startup markdowns or a funding pullback is an ordinary reading. Requiring several months of sustained valuation rises before calling it contradicted is fair, since he named no time frame. Whether Character.AI's lawsuit-driven bankruptcy counts as the trigger is the evaluator's choice.

evidence.note: Character.ai's own announcement of its Chapter 11 filing and court-supervised sale. It shows the antecedent may be met. It says nothing about the outcome.
Confirms the bankruptcy and sale process. The $20m Disney payment is for an IP license, not the price of the company, so it only loosely shows a firesale price.
Earlier valuation history ($1bn Series A), which provides the baseline for calling the sale a firesale.
Nine days after the filing, an AI startup raised $1bn at a quadrupled valuation. This weakly points against a quick break in the market, but it is one deal over a short window.

reviews.rationale: The antecedent plausibly occurred with Character.AI's 12 October bankruptcy sale. That leaves about two weeks before the evaluation date. The contradiction rule needs several months of sustained broad valuation rises, and the support rule needs broad markdowns linked to the event. One large round (e4) shows neither. With no deadline and no conclusive event, the claim is unresolved.
